bills.title: Foreign agent registration, foreign terrorist organizations, and foreign adversaries.
Ban on employer use of automated decision systems.
Various mental health and insurance matters.
Civil liability for child sexual abuse material.

reading.body:
Indiana's legislative activity on AI-adjacent topics clusters around content harms and employment systems rather than infrastructure or compute policy, suggesting the state views AI primarily as a tool that needs behavioral guardrails.

The fourteen bills tracked span digital sexual abuse imagery, automated hiring decisions, foreign adversary registration, and health care administration. Only one bill directly addresses automated decision systems in employment. The rest address harms downstream of AI deployment rather than the systems themselves: child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual intimate images, foreign influence, and health claims processing. This pattern reflects a regulatory posture focused on uses rather than capabilities.

For AI scaling specifically, this tells us Indiana is not considering restrictions on data centers, power consumption, or the physical infrastructure that compute requires. The state's legislation treats AI as software applied to existing domains rather than as a constraint on energy or building capacity. This alignment with the compute-first view means Indiana's framework is unlikely to impede infrastructure development for AI training or inference.

What the data does not show is whether these bills pass, fail, or stall, and therefore what Indiana's actual enforcement posture will be. It captures proposed legislation across early 2026 but not outcomes. The breadth of bills suggests active attention to AI spillovers without revealing whether the state will prioritize any single area or leave most proposals incomplete.
